title: Palaeolithic Arabia
subtitle: 500,000–8,000 BC · Green Corridors, Archaic Hominins and Homo Sapiens Out of Africa

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: No rulers survive this deep — the record is a sequence of site-horizons: archaic hominins, the first Homo sapiens dispersals, and the resettlement after the Ice Age

entries.label: Archaic hominins at Ti's al-Ghadah
entries.hint: Stone tools lie scattered among the butchered bones of elephants, jaguars and water birds at a fossil lakebed in the Nefud — the only dated Middle Pleistocene faunal assemblage known in Arabia. The find pushed the peninsula's hominin record back by at least 100,000 years and showed the interior was a wooded, lake-studded savanna, not desert, when they arrived.
entries.note: Stewart et al., 'Taphonomic and zooarchaeological investigations at the middle Pleistocene site of Ti's al Ghadah', Quaternary Science Reviews (2019); the hominin association is argued in Nature Ecology & Evolution (2020). Species identity of the toolmakers is not established — 'archaic hominin' covers Homo erectus-grade populations, not a named taxon.

entries.label: An Nasim — the oldest dated Acheulean industry in Arabia
entries.hint: Luminescence dating on lake and river sediments at An Nasim fixed a set of finely made handaxes to Marine Isotope Stage 9, a documented humid window — the first time an Arabian handaxe assemblage was tied to an absolute date rather than typology alone.
entries.note: Scerri, Groucutt et al., 'The expansion of Acheulean hominins into the Nefud Desert of Arabia', Scientific Reports (2021), discovered via the Palaeodeserts Project's remote-sensing survey of relict lake basins.

entries.label: Homo sapiens crosses the Nefud — the Alathar footprints
entries.loc: Alathar palaeolake, Nefud Desert, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: Seven footprints pressed into the mud of a shrinking lakeshore, alongside elephant and camel tracks, are the earliest direct evidence of our own species in Arabia. Size and gait indicate a small group — probably several adults and at least one juvenile — walking the lake margin, most likely to drink or forage.
entries.note: Stewart et al., 'Human footprints provide the first direct evidence of Homo sapiens' at Alathar, Science Advances (2020). Attribution to sapiens rather than Neanderthal rests on comparative foot-shape and stature analysis, not skeletal remains — a strong but probabilistic identification.

entries.label: The Nubian Complex reaches Dhofar
entries.hint: A distinctive Levallois core-reduction technique known from Sudan and the Horn of Africa turns up, largely unchanged, in the mountains of southern Oman — a lithic fingerprint for a population that crossed the southern Red Sea or the Bab-el-Mandeb straits rather than the Sinai land bridge.
entries.note: Rose et al., 'The Nubian Complex of Dhofar, Oman: an African Middle Stone Age industry in southern Arabia', PLOS ONE (2011); dated by optically stimulated luminescence. Cross-references the Magan folio (Oman), whose own period begins some 103,000 years later.

entries.label: Al Wusta — a fossil finger bone
entries.loc: Al Wusta palaeolake, Nefud Desert, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: A single, directly dated intermediate phalanx — the only Arabian Homo sapiens fossil of this age — proves modern humans were living around the Nefud's lakes well before the genetically dominant migration out of Africa some 60,000–50,000 years ago. This dispersal, like the Nubian Complex movement, appears to have been a dead end that left no traceable descendants outside Arabia.
entries.note: Groucutt et al., 'Homo sapiens in Arabia by 85,000 years ago', Nature Ecology & Evolution (2018) — a directly dated fossil, the strongest single anchor in this folio.

entries.group: The Return After the Ice Age
entries.label: Playas reform and people return to the Nefud
entries.loc: Jebel Arnaan, Jebel Mleiha and Jebel Misma, southern Nefud, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: After millennia of Ice Age hyper-aridity had emptied northern Arabia, seasonal lakes reappeared around 14,000–13,000 BC and people followed the water back within a few centuries — leaving, this time, monumental engravings of camels, ibex, aurochs and gazelle up to three metres long marking the routes between waterholes.
entries.note: Guagnin et al., 'Monumental rock art illustrates that humans thrived in the Arabian Desert during the Pleistocene–Holocene transition', Nature Communications (2025); the playa chronology (16,000–13,000 BC) from earlier Palaeodeserts Project stratigraphic work.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Almost nothing survives as direct evidence of violence at this scale of time — what little there is speaks to competition between species, not battles between people

entries.label: Hominins and carnivores compete over the same kills
entries.hint: Stone-tool cut-marks and carnivore tooth-marks overlap on the same elephant bones at Ti's al-Ghadah — hominins and large predators (the fossil record includes a jaguar-sized cat) were drawn to, and competed for, the same carcasses at the lake margin.
entries.note: Stewart et al., Quaternary Science Reviews (2019), taphonomic analysis. This is inferred inter-species competition for a resource, not conflict between hominin groups, for which no Arabian evidence yet exists.

entries.label: Dead-end dispersals and the disappearance of earlier populations
entries.hint: Neither the Nubian Complex population in Dhofar nor the Al Wusta and Alathar groups in the Nefud left detectable genetic descendants — each dispersal into Arabia appears to have been absorbed, replaced or extinguished before the genetically successful migration of c.60,000–50,000 BC. What actually happened to these populations — climate attrition, replacement, absorption — is not established.
entries.note: the 'failed dispersal' framing follows Groucutt et al. (2018) and Rose et al. (2011); it is an inference from absence in the genetic record, not a directly observed event, and should be read as such.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: No hierarchy is visible this far back — only the repeated return to the same fixed points in an unstable landscape

entries.label: Persistent places in an unstable landscape
entries.loc: Ti's al-Ghadah and An Nasim, Nefud Desert
entries.hint: Ti's al-Ghadah and An Nasim were revisited across tens of thousands of years and multiple humid phases — not single episodes but recurring anchor points fixed by a permanent water source, the closest thing this record offers to territorial memory.
entries.note: the 'persistent place' framing is the excavators' own (Stewart et al. 2019; Scerri et al. 2021); it describes repeated reuse of a location, not continuous occupation or social memory in any literal sense.

entries.label: The band as the only visible social unit
entries.hint: Nothing in this record — no monumental architecture, no wealth differentiation in a grave, no specialised craft workshop — implies anything beyond small, mobile foraging bands. Social complexity in Arabia, when it appears, belongs to the folio that follows this one.
entries.note: an argument from absence rather than a positive finding; stated explicitly so it is not mistaken for a gap in research rather than a genuine feature of the evidence.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: No confirmed symbolic behaviour is yet documented for this period in Arabia — a gap worth stating plainly rather than filling with inference

entries.label: No confirmed art, ornament or deliberate burial
entries.hint: Unlike contemporary sites in Africa (engraved ochre, shell beads) or Europe (cave art, deliberate burial), no Arabian site of this age has yet produced confirmed symbolic material culture. This may reflect the state of research and the destructive climate history as much as an absence of the practice itself.
entries.note: stated as an honest gap, following the same caution the Nubian Complex and Alathar papers themselves apply to absence-of-evidence claims; future fieldwork could overturn it at any time.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: One find, right at the end of this folio's span, changes the picture entirely: monumental rock art marking the water sources of the resettled Nefud

entries.label: Monumental engravings at Jebel Arnaan, Mleiha and Misma
entries.hint: Across three newly surveyed outcrops, more than 60 panels carry 176 engravings — camels, ibex, gazelle, aurochs and wild equids, some over three metres long, life-sized and naturalistically rendered — cut into rock faces that stood beside the resettlement-era lakes as markers of water and route.
entries.note: Guagnin et al., Nature Communications (2025). The oldest large-scale monumental rock art securely dated in Arabia, roughly two millennia before the earliest built stone monuments (the mustatils) that follow it.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: What this folio knows, it knows entirely from method — luminescence dating, speleothem chemistry and comparative footprint anatomy, not a single written word

entries.label: Speleothems record eight million years of climate
entries.hint: Uranium-series dating of 22 stalagmites from seven cave systems reconstructed a cycle of humid and arid phases stretching back 7.44 million years — the deep-time backbone against which every human dispersal into Arabia is now measured, and evidence that these wet phases grew shorter and weaker as the planet cooled.
entries.note: 'Recurrent humid phases in Arabia over the past 8 million years', Nature (2025), an international team supported by Saudi Arabia's Heritage Commission. This is a climate-methods entry, not itself a human-occupation record.

entries.label: Luminescence dating opens the Pleistocene record
entries.loc: An Nasim, Nefud Desert; Aybut al-Auwal, Oman
entries.hint: Optically stimulated luminescence — measuring the last time buried quartz grains saw sunlight — gave An Nasim's handaxes and the Nubian Complex tools of Dhofar their first absolute dates, moving Arabian prehistory from typological guesswork to a chronometric science within a single decade.
entries.note: the method underlies Rose et al. (2011) and Scerri et al. (2021) alike; both papers foreground the dating method as their central methodological contribution.

entries.label: Reading a species from a footprint
entries.hint: With no bones to examine, the Alathar team identified the footprint-makers as Homo sapiens by comparing print size, shape and estimated stature and gait against a reference set of known human and Neanderthal tracks — a method that turns an ichnological trace into a taxonomic argument.
entries.note: Stewart et al., Science Advances (2020); the identification is comparative and probabilistic, a genuine methodological limit the paper itself acknowledges.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: A hunting-and-foraging economy tied absolutely to the lake margin — and, twice, a hyper-arid collapse that emptied the interior of people entirely

entries.label: Megafauna hunting and scavenging at the lake edge
entries.hint: Butchered elephant, hippopotamus and water-bird bones at Ti's al-Ghadah show hominins working large and dangerous prey at the water's edge — whether by active hunting or aggressive scavenging is debated, but the diet was clearly built around the animals a permanent lake could support.
entries.note: Stewart et al., Quaternary Science Reviews (2019).

entries.label: A foraging economy that follows the lake, not the season
entries.hint: Every dated site in this folio — Ti's al-Ghadah, An Nasim, Alathar, Al Wusta — sits on a former lakeshore. Arabian foragers of this era were not desert specialists; they were lake-margin foragers whose entire range contracted or vanished with the water.
entries.note: a synthesis observation drawn from the site pattern common to Stewart et al. (2019, 2020), Groucutt et al. (2018) and Scerri et al. (2021).

entries.label: The Last Glacial Maximum empties northern Arabia
entries.hint: Hyper-aridity from roughly 25,000 BC mobilised the dune fields and drove out or killed off the human population of northern Arabia; no dated archaeological site anywhere in the region falls within this multi-millennium window.
entries.note: the archaeological silence is documented in the Palaeodeserts Project's regional survey record, most recently summarised in Guagnin et al., Nature Communications (2025), which frames the following recovery against it.

entries.label: The Nefud's playas reform and people return
entries.hint: Seasonal lakes (playas) re-established across the Nefud from around 14,000 BC — the first standing water there since the Last Glacial Maximum — and stratified camp sites dated to 12,800–11,400 BC show people moved back in within a few centuries of the water's return.
entries.note: Guagnin et al., Nature Communications (2025), citing earlier Palaeodeserts Project stratigraphic dating of the playa sediments.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Two named toolmaking traditions carry almost the whole record: the Acheulean handaxe and the African-derived Nubian Complex point

entries.label: Acheulean façonnage at An Nasim
entries.hint: The An Nasim handaxes are finely shaped by façonnage — flaking a whole cobble down to a symmetrical biface — a technique that varies regionally across Arabia and shows Middle Pleistocene hominins here were not using a single uniform toolkit but locally distinct traditions.
entries.note: Scerri, Groucutt et al., Scientific Reports (2021).

entries.label: Nubian Levallois point production
entries.hint: The Nubian Complex is a specific way of preparing a stone core to strike an elongated, triangular point in a single blow — a technique otherwise known only from Sudan and the Horn of Africa, carried into Arabia essentially unchanged and used here as a fingerprint for the population that made it.
entries.note: Rose et al., PLOS ONE (2011).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Arabia as a corridor rather than a destination — repeatedly crossed, in both directions, by populations moving between Africa and the rest of Eurasia

entries.label: Arabia as the Africa–Eurasia crossroads
entries.hint: The 2025 speleothem study frames its own eight-million-year record explicitly as evidence that Arabia's recurring humid windows opened a corridor for mammal (and hominin) exchange between Africa and Eurasia — a 'hitherto unrecognised' biogeographic crossroads operating on a timescale far longer than any single human dispersal.
entries.note: 'Recurrent humid phases in Arabia over the past 8 million years', Nature (2025).

entries.label: The northern route — Sinai, the Levant and the Nefud
entries.loc: the Sinai land bridge and Nefud Desert
entries.hint: The Alathar footprints and the Al Wusta finger bone sit on the other plausible corridor out of Africa — the Sinai land bridge into the Levant and down into northern Arabia — the route later used by the successful c.60,000 BC dispersal that populated the rest of the world.
entries.note: Groucutt et al. (2018); Stewart et al. (2020).

entries.label: Dead ends: the dispersals that left no descendants
entries.hint: Genetic studies of living populations find no trace of the Nubian Complex, Al Wusta or Alathar groups — each appears to have been a successful but ultimately dead-end colonisation, absorbed or extinguished before the one dispersal, around 60,000–50,000 BC, whose descendants are alive today.
entries.note: the 'multiple dispersal, one success' model is argued across Groucutt et al. (2018), Stewart et al. (2020) and the broader Out-of-Africa genetics literature; it remains a live area of research, not a settled conclusion.

entries.label: The southern route — Bab-el-Mandeb and the Nubian Complex
entries.loc: the Bab-el-Mandeb strait and Dhofar, Oman
entries.hint: The Nubian Complex's presence in Dhofar, otherwise known only in North-East Africa, is the strongest single piece of evidence for a population crossing directly from the Horn of Africa into southern Arabia — a route distinct from, and probably earlier than, the northern Sinai crossing.
entries.note: Rose et al., PLOS ONE (2011); the routing argument is inferential, based on the lithic technology's African affinities rather than a directly traced migration path.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: A desert that was, for most of the last eight million years, something closer to a savanna — and the long, uneven slide toward the aridity of today

entries.label: Eight million years of 'Green Arabia'
entries.hint: Long before any hominin arrived, Arabia was already cycling between desert and a 'green paradise' of permanent lakes, rivers, woodland and grassland — a pattern driven by slow shifts in Earth's orbit, recorded in cave stalagmites, and repeating for millions of years before humans ever crossed it.
entries.note: Nature (2025), the speleothem study.

entries.label: A one-way trend toward aridity
entries.hint: Each humid cycle in the speleothem record is shorter and weaker than the one before it, tracking the wider global cooling of the last several million years — the ancient lakes of this folio were not a stable backdrop but a slowly failing one, and the modern Empty Quarter is where that trend has, for now, arrived.
entries.note: Nature (2025).

entries.label: The handoff to a settled Holocene
entries.hint: By the start of the Holocene the pattern that had governed Arabia for eight million years repeats one last time at human scale: the monsoon shifts north, the interior turns green, and — for the first time — people stay through it, building the herding, ritual and eventually walled-town societies this folio's successor covers.
entries.note: the Holocene Humid Period is picked up in detail as the opening entry of the Gulf-prehistory folio and of the Neolithic Hejaz folio that follow this one.

entries.label: A 42-metre lake in the Empty Quarter
entries.hint: A separate 2025 study traced a freshwater lake more than 1,100 km2 in area and 42 metres deep in the heart of what is now the Empty Quarter — fed by monsoon rains during the early Holocene humid phase, and large enough that its overflow cut a valley 150 km long across the desert floor.
entries.note: Afifi, Delaunay, Baby and Zaki (KAUST and the University of Geneva), 2025. A different, later study from the 8-million-year speleothem paper — the two are often conflated in popular coverage but reconstruct different features on different timescales.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: A handful of footprints and a single bone are the closest this folio comes to an individual life — everyone else is visible only as an anonymous population

entries.label: The invisible majority of a mobile world
entries.hint: Every named site in this folio is a rare accident of preservation at a former lakebed; the actual population — small mobile bands moving across a vast interior — left almost no trace at all. The handful of footprints, one bone and a few stone scatters represent, at best, a tiny fraction of the people who lived and died here across half a million years.
entries.note: a framing observation rather than a single citable finding — the point made explicitly by Petraglia and colleagues across the Palaeodeserts Project's publications on survey bias.

entries.label: The footprint-makers of Alathar
entries.hint: Seven footprints — probably several adults and at least one child, moving together across drying mud — are as close as this record comes to watching specific, named-less people cross a landscape. Nothing else about them (their band, their language, their fate) survives.
entries.note: Stewart et al., Science Advances (2020).

entries.label: One finger, one person, 85,000 years ago
entries.hint: The entire physical trace of this individual is a single bone from a finger — enough to identify the species, date the find and rewrite the migration timeline, but nothing about the person who once used that hand.
entries.note: Groucutt et al., Nature Ecology & Evolution (2018).
